entities.summary:
Stabat Mater, a poignant and theologically rich poem, is attributed to Jacopone da Todi, a 13th-century Italian Franciscan friar, and is believed to have been composed around 1280. This literary work emerged within the context of the medieval church's evolving relationship with the laity and the growing emphasis on personal piety and devotion. It holds immense significance in Christian liturgical traditions, particularly in the Catholic Church, where it is used in the context of the Feast of Our Lady of Sorrows. Stabat Mater encapsulates the profound sorrow Mary experienced during the crucifixion of Jesus, reflecting the human condition and suffering, key themes that resonate throughout the history of Christian thought.

The text, structured as a sequence of 20 stanzas, became integral to the liturgical practice of the church, especially during the Lent and Holy Week. Its impact was further amplified in the 17th century when composers such as Giovanni Battista Pergolesi set the text to music, creating a masterful oratorio that popularized the work across Europe. This adaptation brought Stabat Mater into the concert hall, bridging the gap between sacred and secular music, and ensuring its enduring legacy in Western music culture. The poem's emotional depth and vivid imagery have inspired countless artistic interpretations across various media, including paintings, sculptures, and operas.

Their legacy is studied through the lens of historical causation.", "summary": "The Stabat Mater (Latin: 'The Mother Was Standing') is a medieval Catholic hymn attributed to the Italian Franciscan poet Jacopone da Todi (c. 1230–1306 CE), composed c. 1290–1300 CE and one of the most celebrated and widely set texts in the history of Western sacred music. The hymn consists of 20 stanzas in rhymed Latin verse describing the grief of the Virgin Mary at the foot of the cross during the crucifixion of Jesus — presenting a meditation on compassion (compassio), suffering, and the devotion of the believer who seeks to share in Mary's grief and in Christ's passion. The hymn begins: 'Stabat mater dolorosa / Iuxta crucem lacrimosa / Dum pendebat filius' ('The grieving mother was standing / Weeping beside the cross / While her Son was hanging there').

The Stabat Mater was widely used in Catholic liturgy and devotion — it was adopted as a sequence for the Feast of the Seven Sorrows of Our Lady and for the Stations of the Cross. Its text was set to music by virtually every major European composer from the 14th century to the 20th: Giovanni da Palestrina (c. 1590), Agostino Steffani, Alessandro Scarlatti, Vivaldi (1712), Pergolesi (1736 — the most performed setting, composed in the last weeks of his life), Haydn (1767), Boccherini, Schubert (1816), Rossini (1832/1841), Dvořák (1877), Verdi (1898), and Poulenc (1950/1951), among many others — making it the most multiply-composed Latin text other than the Mass and the Magnificat.

The Stabat Mater is a supreme expression of medieval Franciscan affective piety — the devotional tradition, pioneered by Francis of Assisi and his followers, that emphasised emotional identification with the suffering Christ and the grieving Mary as the primary method of spiritual growth. Its influence extended beyond Catholic devotion to Protestant musical culture (J.S.
